meta.title: Yorùbá Yé Mi — A Beginning Yorùbá Textbook
meta.author: Fẹ̀hìntọ́lá Mosádomi, Ph.D — COERLL, The University of Texas at Austin (2012)
extractionNotes: The PDF uses a legacy 'YorubaSans' font with no Unicode mapping; all Yorùbá diacritics (ọ, ẹ, ṣ, tone marks) were recovered via an empirically derived character map (see decode.py). Spot-checked across all 12 chapters, but isolated mis-decoded characters may remain.
Vocabulary was extracted positionally from the two-column 'Àwọn ọ̀rọ̀' tables of each chapter (1,008 entries). English glosses that wrapped across lines were rejoined automatically.

Grammar explanations are concise summaries written from each lesson's content; example sentences are harvested verbatim from the book's two-column example tables. Lessons that are mostly dialogue/exercise pages yielded few or no machine-extractable example pairs (notably ch. 7–9, 12 later lessons).
Dialogues (Ìsọ̀rọ̀ngbèsì) and in-book exercises (Iṣẹ́ Ṣíṣe) were not separately structured; the app generates its own drills from vocab + grammar items instead.
The book's Introduction (alphabet, tones, pronunciation) is included as reference material, not as a gated chapter.
The textbook has no bundled audio; COERLL hosts audio for this book online, but the app is offline-first so listening drills are omitted.

intro.title: Introduction: The Sounds of Yorùbá
notes: Yorùbá has 7 oral vowels: a, e, ẹ (as in 'bet'), i, o, ọ (as in 'bought'), u — plus nasal vowels: an, ẹn, in, ọn, un.
Three tones distinguish word meanings: High (á, marked ´), Mid (a, unmarked), Low (à, marked `). Example: bí 'to give birth', bi 'to ask', bì 'to vomit'.
Consonants include gb (a single sound, pronounced together), ṣ (like English 'sh'), p (pronounced [kp]), and j (like English 'j'). There is no c, q, v, x or z.
The syllabic nasals ń/ǹ can form syllables on their own and carry tone, e.g. ń in Ó ń lọ 'He is going'.

items.title: Ìkíni (Greetings)
items.explanation: Greetings are formed with kú + a time of day or occasion, and contract: kú + àárọ̀ → káàárọ̀ 'good morning'. Add Ẹ before a greeting to show respect or address more than one person (Ẹ káàárọ̀). The times of day are àárọ̀ (morning), ọ̀sán (afternoon), ìrọ̀lẹ́ (early evening) and alẹ́ (night).

items.title: Verbs
items.explanation: Yorùbá verbs are not inflected: the same form serves every person and tense (lọ = go/went). Negation uses kò before the verb: Kò lọ 'He/she did not go'. The progressive uses ń before the verb: Ó ń sùn 'He/she is sleeping'.

items.title: Subject Pronouns
items.explanation: Short subject pronouns: mo (I), o (you sg.), ó (he/she/it), a (we), ẹ (you pl./respect), wọ́n (they/respect). Emphatic pronouns: èmi, ìwọ, òun, àwa, ẹ̀yin, àwọn.

Ẹ̀yin ń sùn / Ẹ̀ ń sùn

items.title: Interrogatives 'Kí ni?' and 'Ṣé?'
items.explanation: Kí ni…? asks 'what is…?' (Kí ni orúkọ rẹ? 'What is your name?'). Ṣé turns a statement into a yes/no question: Ṣé dáadáa ni? 'Are you fine?' Answer with bẹ́ẹ̀ ni (yes) or bẹ́ẹ̀ kọ́ / ó tì (no).

examples.yo: R: Bẹ́ẹ̀ ni, wọ́n fẹ́ owó.
R: Bẹ́ẹ́ ni, mo fẹ́ jẹun.
Wálé fẹ́ jẹ ìrẹsì, ó sì fẹ́

items.title: Possessive Pronouns
items.explanation: Possessives follow the noun, whose final vowel lengthens: ìwéè mi 'my book', iléè rẹ̀ 'his/her house'. Forms: mi (my), rẹ/ẹ (your sg.), rẹ̀/ẹ̀ (his/her/its), wa (our), yín (your pl.), wọn (their). Wọn and yín also mark respect for elders and superiors.

items.title: The plural marker 'àwọn'
items.explanation: Nouns do not change form for number. Plurality is shown by placing àwọn before the noun: àwọn ìwé 'books', àwọn akẹ́kọ̀ọ́ 'students'.

examples.yo: Mo ri àwọn obìnrin náà lánàá
Àwọn ọkùnrin máa ń dé fìlà

items.title: Nínú Kíláàsì (In the Classroom)
items.explanation: Classroom objects and commands. The preposition ní 'in/at/on' contracts with nouns: ní + inú → nínú 'inside', ní + ilé → nílé 'at home'. Common commands: dìde 'stand up', jókòó 'sit down', tẹ́tí sílẹ̀ 'listen'.

examples.en: in between / in the middle of

items.title: Nọ́ńbà (Numbers 0–40)
items.explanation: Counting forms: oókan (1), eéjì (2), ẹẹ́ta (3), ẹẹ́rin (4), aárùnún (5), ẹẹ́fà (6), eéje (7), ẹẹ́jọ (8), ẹẹ́sànán (9), ẹẹ́wàá (10)… ogún (20), ọgbọ̀n (30), ogójì (40). Qualifying numerals take m-: ìwé mẹ́ta 'three books'.

chapters.title: Mark the Date
objectives: How to ask how much…, how many..., and what is the sum of?
How to identify the days of the week and months of the year

items.title: Nọ́ńbà (Numbers 40–100)
items.explanation: Yorùbá counts in twenties: ogójì (40), àádọ́ta (50 = 60−10), ọgọ́ta (60), àádọ́rin (70), ọgọ́rin (80), àádọ́rùnún (90), ọgọ́rùnún (100). Tens between are formed by subtraction from the next twenty.

items.title: Future Tense 'máa'
items.explanation: The future is marked with máa (or yóò) before the verb: Màá lọ / Èmi máa lọ 'I will go'; Wọ́n máa jẹun 'They will eat'.

examples.en: You all (or honorific singular) will go

items.title: Days of the Week
items.explanation: The seven days: Ọjọ́ Àìkú (Sunday), Ọjọ́ Ajé (Monday), Ọjọ́ Ìṣẹ́gun (Tuesday), Ọjọ́rú (Wednesday), Ọjọ́bọ̀ (Thursday), Ọjọ́ Ẹtì (Friday), Ọjọ́ Àbámẹ́ta (Saturday). Ọjọ́ 'day' precedes most names.

items.title: Months of the Year (Kàlẹ́ńdà Yorùbá)
items.explanation: Months use oṣù 'month' + ordinal: Oṣù Kìíní 'January (first month)', Oṣù Kejì 'February', … Oṣù Kejìlá 'December (twelfth month)'.

examples.en: second month of the year February

items.title: The Interrogative 'Mélòó'
items.explanation: Mélòó asks 'how many?' after a (singular) noun: Ìwé mélòó? 'How many books?' Answers use qualifying numerals: ìwé mẹ́ta 'three books'.

examples.yo: Ìwé mélòó ni ó wà ní oríi tábìlì?
examples.en: How many books are on the table?

examples.yo: Ìwé mẹ́ta ni ó wà lóríi tábìlì
examples.en: There are three books on the table.

items.title: Aago mélòó ni ó lù? (What time is it?)
items.explanation: Time is asked with Aago mélòó ni ó lù? 'What time has struck?' Answers: aago méje (7 o'clock); ààbọ̀ 'half past' (aago méje àábọ̀); ìṣẹ́jú 'minute' with lé 'past' and kù 'to': ó ku ìṣẹ́jú mẹ́wàá kí aago mẹ́jọ 'ten to eight'.

examples.en: from about 7:00 pm to 10:00 or 11:59 pm

items.title: Asking for Age
items.explanation: Age uses ọdún 'year': Ọmọ ọdún mélòó ni ọ́? 'How old are you?' — Ọmọ ọdún mẹ́rìndínlógún ni mí 'I am sixteen years old'.

items.title: Àwọn Àwọ̀ (Colors)
items.explanation: Core color terms: funfun 'white', dúdú 'black/dark', pupa 'red/light-complexioned'. Other colors are described with phrases, e.g. àwọ̀ ewé 'leaf-colored (green)', àwọ̀ ọ̀run 'sky-colored (blue)'.

examples.en: S/he/ It is black/dark like a leaf (green color)
S/he/ it is dark/black like charcoal

items.title: The verbs 'jẹ́' and 'ni' (to be)
items.explanation: Both mean 'to be'. Ni is equative and follows the complement: Olùkọ́ ni mí 'I am a teacher'. Jẹ́ precedes the complement: Mo jẹ́ olùkọ́. The negation of ni is kọ́: Olùkọ́ kọ́ ni mí 'I am not a teacher'.

examples.yo: Ẹ̀wà jẹ́ oúnjẹ tí ó dára láti jẹ
Màmáà mi jẹ́ ọmọ ogójì ọdún

items.title: The interrogative 'Ta ni'
items.explanation: Ta ni…? asks 'who is…?': Ta ni èyí? 'Who is this?' — Bàbáà mi ni 'It is my father'.

examples.yo: Bàbá Ọlá: Ìyẹn dára o. Ta ni ọ̀rẹ́ẹ̀ rẹ?
examples.en: That’s nice. Who is your friend?

items.title: Ẹbí ní ìdílé Mẹ́ta (Three Generations of a Family)
items.explanation: Family terms: bàbá 'father', ìyá/màmá 'mother', ẹ̀gbọ́n 'older sibling', àbúrò 'younger sibling' (no gender distinction), ọmọ 'child', ìyá àgbà 'grandmother', bàbá àgbà 'grandfather'. Seniority, not gender, organizes sibling terms.

items.title: Describing People
items.explanation: Descriptive verbs/adjectives: ga 'be tall', kúrú 'be short', tóbi 'be big', kéré 'be small', sanra 'be fat', tínrín 'be thin'; used directly as predicates: Ó ga 'He/she is tall'.

examples.en: S/he is neither tall nor short

items.title: Interrogative 'Eélòó'
items.explanation: Eélòó asks 'how much?': Eélòó ni? 'How much is it?' — Ogún náírà ni 'It is twenty naira (₦20)'.

items.title: Oní-/Al-/Ẹl-/Ọl- (owner/seller prefix)
items.explanation: The prefix oní- 'owner/seller of' assimilates to the noun's first vowel: oní + ata → aláta 'pepper seller'; oní + ẹja → ẹlẹ́ja 'fish seller'; oní + ọtí → ọlọ́tí 'drink seller'; before i/consonant it stays oní-: oníṣòwò 'trader'.

examples.en: one who sells or fixes watches

items.title: Níná Ọjà (Haggling)
items.explanation: Market bargaining: Eélòó ni? 'how much?', Ó wọ́n jù 'it is too expensive', Dín owó rẹ̀ kù 'reduce the price', Mo fẹ́ raà á 'I want to buy it'.

items.title: Nọ́ńbà (Numbers 100–3000)
items.explanation: Large numbers: ọgọ́rùnún (100), igba (200), ọ̀ọ́dúnrún (300), irinwó (400), ẹ̀ẹ́dẹ́gbẹ̀ta (500), ẹgbẹ̀ta (600), ẹgbẹ̀rún (1000), ẹgbàá (2000), ẹgbẹ̀ẹ́dógún (3000).

items.title: Verbs 'fẹ́' and 'fẹ́ràn'
items.explanation: Fẹ́ = 'to want' (also 'to love'); fẹ́ràn = 'to like/love'. Fẹ́ + verb expresses 'want to': Mo fẹ́ jẹun 'I want to eat'. Mo fẹ́ràn ìrẹsì 'I like rice'.

items.title: Àwọn oúnjẹ òòjọ́ (Daily meals)
items.explanation: Meals: oúnjẹ àárọ̀ 'breakfast', oúnjẹ ọ̀sán 'lunch', oúnjẹ alẹ́ 'dinner'. Hunger and thirst are expressed with 'pa' and 'gbẹ': Ebi ń pa mí 'I am hungry', Òùngbẹ ń gbẹ mí 'I am thirsty'.

items.title: In the Market
items.explanation: Buying and selling food: ra 'to buy', ta 'to sell', ọjà 'market'. Mo fẹ́ ra ẹja 'I want to buy fish'. Names of staple foods: iṣu 'yam', ìrẹsì 'rice', ẹ̀wà 'beans', ọ̀gẹ̀dẹ̀ 'banana/plantain'.

items.title: Rírà oúnjẹ nínúu búkà (Ordering food in a restaurant)
items.explanation: In a búkà (local restaurant): Kí ni ẹ ní? 'What do you have?', Fún mi ní… 'Give me…', Mo fẹ́ jẹ iṣu àti ẹyin 'I want to eat yam and eggs'.

items.title: Possessive forms of emphatic pronouns
items.explanation: Ti + possessive gives 'mine/yours/…': tèmi 'mine', tìrẹ 'yours (sg.)', tirẹ̀ 'his/hers/its', tiwa 'ours', tiyín 'yours (pl.)', tiwọn 'theirs': Ìwé yìí tèmi ni 'This book is mine'.

items.title: Parts of the Body
items.explanation: Body parts: orí 'head', ojú 'eye/face', imú 'nose', ẹnu 'mouth', etí 'ear', ọrùn 'neck', apá 'arm', ọwọ́ 'hand', ikùn 'stomach', ẹsẹ̀ 'leg/foot', orúkún 'knee', ìka 'finger/toe'.

items.title: Ìlera àti àìsàn (Health and illness)
items.explanation: Talking about health: Ara mi ń ro mí 'my body aches', orí ń fọ́ mi 'I have a headache', inú ń run mí 'I have a stomachache'. Àìsàn 'illness', ìlera 'health', dókítà 'doctor', oògùn 'medicine'.

items.title: Eré Ìdárayá (Sports)
items.explanation: Sports and exercise: eré ìdárayá 'sports/recreation', gba bọ́ọ̀lù 'play ball', sáré 'run', wẹ̀ 'swim/bathe'. Máa followed by verb also expresses habitual future activity.

items.title: Verbs for Professions
items.explanation: Professions use jẹ́ or ṣe + occupation: Mo jẹ́ dókítà / Mo ń ṣiṣẹ́ dókítà 'I am a doctor / I work as a doctor'. Ń ṣiṣẹ́ = 'is working'.

examples.en: What do you want to become?

items.title: Negation: 'kò tí ì' / 'kò ì tí ì'
items.explanation: Kò tí ì (or kò ì tí ì) + verb means 'has not (yet)': Kò tí ì dé 'He/she has not yet arrived'; Wọn kò ì tí ì jẹun 'They have not yet eaten'.

items.title: Professions
items.explanation: Many profession nouns are derived with prefixes a- or oní-: akọ̀wé 'clerk/secretary', agbẹ̀ 'farmer', oníṣòwò 'trader', awakọ̀ 'driver', olùkọ́ 'teacher', dókítà 'doctor', lọ́yà 'lawyer'.

items.en: ‘don’t buy matches’ (it's a type of window)

items.title: Ordinals
items.explanation: Ordinals prefix k- to the numeral: kìíní 'first', kejì 'second', kẹta 'third', kẹrin 'fourth'… Ilé kìíní 'the first house'. Noun forms take è-/ì-: èkínní, èkejì.

items.title: Reflexives and Vowel Processes
items.explanation: Reflexives use ara + possessive: ara mi 'myself', ara rẹ̀ 'himself/herself'. Yorùbá speech shows vowel assimilation (ilé + ẹ̀ → iléè), vowel lengthening in possessive constructions, and vowel deletion in rapid speech (kí + ó → kó).

Màmáà mi ya irunùn mi fún mi.
examples.en: My mother combed my hair for me.

examples.en: My mother helped me comb my hair.

items.title: Aṣọ wíwọ̀ ní ilẹ̀ẹ Yorùbá (Types of Clothing)
items.explanation: Traditional dress: bùbá 'blouse/shirt', ìró 'wrap skirt', gèlè 'head-tie', ṣòkòtò 'trousers', agbádá 'flowing gown', fìlà 'cap', bàtà 'shoes'.

items.title: More Interrogatives
items.explanation: Further question words: Irú … wo? 'which kind of…?', Níbo? 'where?', Báwo? 'how?': Irú aṣọ wo ni o fẹ́? 'Which kind of cloth do you want?'

items.title: Seasonal Clothings
items.explanation: Clothing follows the seasons: heavy cloth (aṣọ tí ó wúwo) for òtútù 'the cold/rainy season', light cloth (aṣọ fẹ́lẹ́fẹ́lẹ́) for ẹ̀rùn 'the dry/hot season'.

items.title: Ilé-Ìwé (School System)
items.explanation: School vocabulary: ilé-ìwé 'school', ilé-ìwé alákọ̀ọ́bẹ̀rẹ̀ 'primary school', ilé-ìwé girama 'secondary school', yunifásítì/fásitì 'university', akẹ́kọ̀ọ́ 'student', olùkọ́ 'teacher'.

items.title: Campus Life
items.explanation: Describing daily life on campus: classes, studying (kàwé 'to read/study'), friends, and activities, combining the chapter's vocabulary with earlier grammar.
